title: Why rites
hook: rites are patterns of worship that carry memory in bodies

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last page: a garden at the front of the Bible, a city at the back. Your line was from garden to city.

A cake comes out of a dark kitchen with candles burning. Somebody starts a song, and everyone joins on the second note. The birthday person leans in, makes a wish, and blows. Nobody hands out instructions or explains what the candles mean. Hands clap at the right moment anyway, because they've done this before, and somebody did it for them. That little pattern holds years of birthdays inside it. A new block begins here: church life, its rites, spaces and arts. And it starts with a question: why do Christians worship in patterns at all?

A rite is a pattern of worship you do, not just say: words, yes, but also bread, water, standing, kneeling, walking forward. The Bible is full of them. Start with a question a child asks. In Exodus, God tells Israel how to keep the Passover, and adds: "when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service?" The rite comes first. The question comes later, from a small person at the table who has watched it happen. Jewish families still keep that night, and a child at the table still asks. Next, a meal at that same feast. Luke tells how Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and says: "This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me." Do. Not think about, not agree with. Do. Christians still keep that meal, in many shapes, and the coming days walk through several of them. Third, the body joins in. Paul writes, "For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father." A psalm says, "Lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD." Knees and hands are part of the prayer. Churches differ on how much pattern they keep. Some are rich with it: incense, processions, the sign of the cross. Others keep it plain on purpose, and some keep almost none. Even a plain church tends to have its own way of doing things that newcomers notice right away. A tired mind can forget a sermon. Knees that have bent in the same place for years carry something too. Hands remember where to go.
screen: `A PATTERN YOU DO, NOT JUST SAY.`

segments.voice: Look for a pattern you repeat without thinking: the first cup of the day, a goodnight said the same way, a grave you visit and what you do there. Walk through one slowly in your mind, notice what your hands do, and ask who taught it to you. If you pray, bring that pattern to God and give thanks for whoever started it.
Rite. Worship done with the body as well as said: bread broken, water poured, knees bent.
Your line: bodies remember. A pattern can hold what words let slip. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians worship through rites such as baptism and the Lord's Supper, and many churches also kneel, stand, bow, raise hands or make the sign of the cross at set points in a service; how much pattern a church keeps varies widely.

fork.setup: you're a child at the Passover table, watching the grown-ups do something they've done every year. what happens next, in Exodus?

you ask, "what mean ye by this service?"

fork.reveal: Exodus expects the child to ask, and the grown-ups to answer. the rite opens the question.

chat.says: Why do some churches repeat the same rituals every week? Isn't that just going through the motions?
options: A rite is worship you do with your body; like a birthday song, the pattern carries meaning.
Rites are just habit; the Bible never mentions worship done with the body.
Rites are only for children; in Exodus, grown-ups stop once they understand.
chat.meaning: A rite is worship you do as well as say. Jesus says this do in remembrance of me, and knees and hands join the prayer: bodies remember.
